hints: Start by picturing the axon at rest - no impulse. What is the charge difference across the membrane, inside compared to outside?
Think about what protein in the membrane constantly works to keep Na+ mostly outside and K+ mostly inside, even at rest.
Recall how that pump is powered and why it needs energy - what type of transport moves ions against their concentration gradients?
Remember the pump does not move equal numbers - think 3 of one ion one way and 2 of the other the other way. How would that alone affect charge?
Now think about leak channels - which ion can leak back much more easily at rest, and what happens to charge when positive ions leave?
Do not forget what is trapped inside the axon that cannot cross, and the final voltage value you should quote for resting potential.
walkthrough:
Set the scene - inside negative at rest**
Think of the axon membrane like a battery waiting to fire. At rest the inside is negative compared to the outside, about -70 $mV$. That negativity has to be created and held all the time. Two things do it together: pumps and leaks.

The sodium-potassium pump builds the gradients**
Embedded in the membrane are sodium-potassium pumps. They use ATP for active transport because they push ions against their concentration gradients. Each cycle pumps 3 $Na^+$ out of the axon and 2 $K^+$ into the axon. Because 3 positive charges leave for every 2 that enter, this directly makes the inside more negative and sets up both concentration and electrochemical gradients - high $Na^+$ outside, high $K^+$ inside.

Differential permeability lets K+ leak out**
At rest the membrane is much more permeable to $K^+$ than to $Na^+$ because there are many more open $K^+$ channels. So $K^+$ diffuses out down its concentration gradient faster than $Na^+$ can diffuse in. That net loss of positive ions from inside adds to the negativity.

Trapped anions lock in the negativity**
Inside the cytoplasm there are large negatively charged proteins and other anions that are too big to cross the membrane. They stay inside and contribute to the negative interior. Together pump activity, $K^+$ loss and trapped anions maintain a steady resting potential of about -60 to -70 $mV$.

Final answer: Sodium-potassium pumps transport $Na^+$ out and $K^+$ in by active transport using ATP, 3 $Na^+$ out for 2 $K^+$ in; sets up electrochemical gradient. Membrane is more permeable to $K^+$ with more $K^+$ channels, so more $K^+$ diffuses out than $Na^+$ diffuses in. Negatively charged proteins / anions remain inside, so inside is negative relative to outside at -60 to -70 $mV$.

hints: First line up the two graphs side by side. Compare the flat starting lines before time 1 ms - what are the resting values in Fig. 7.1 and Fig. 7.2?
Now follow the spike up and down. Look at how far up it goes from rest and how long the whole spike lasts in normal versus hypokalaemia.
Finally look at the dip below resting after the spike. Compare its depth and duration, and remember to support each difference with paired numbers from the axes.
walkthrough:
Compare resting potentials first**
Look at the flat line before the impulse. In Fig. 7.1 normal it sits at -70 $mV$. In Fig. 7.2 hypokalaemia it sits much lower at -100 $mV$. So resting potential is more negative. Always give both numbers with units $mV$ - that is your data quote.

Compare the action potential spike**
Now trace the upstroke and downstroke. In hypokalaemia the spike starts from a lower baseline but still reaches +40 $mV$, so the total depolarisation is larger, about 140 $mV$ compared to about 110 $mV$ normal. It is also slower: depolarisation lasts about 1.25 $ms$ versus 1.0 $ms$, repolarisation about 1.3 $ms$ versus 1.0 $ms$, so total action potential about 3.25 $ms$ versus 2.6 $ms$.

Compare hyperpolarisation**
Look at the dip after the spike. In normal it dips to about -92 $mV$, only about 22 $mV$ below rest, for about 0.7 $ms$. In hypokalaemia it dips to about -112 $mV$, about 12 $mV$ below its rest, and lasts longer, about 1.0 $ms$. You can describe this as more negative and longer hyperpolarisation. Pick any three well-evidenced differences with paired figures to earn full credit.

Final answer: Resting potential more negative in hypokalaemia, -100 $mV$ vs -70 $mV$ normal. Longer / larger depolarisation in hypokalaemia, e.g. depolarisation 1.25 $ms$ vs 1.0 $ms$ normal and rise of 140 $mV$ vs 110 $mV$; longer repolarisation 1.3 $ms$ vs 1.0 $ms$. Longer and more negative hyperpolarisation, e.g. to -112 $mV$ for 1.0 $ms$ vs -92 $mV$ for 0.7 $ms$ normal.

hints: Think about what must happen to go from that very negative resting value up to threshold - does it need a smaller or larger change than normal?
If each impulse is harder to start and takes longer, what does that mean for how many impulses can travel and how fast muscles or the brain can respond?
walkthrough:
Harder to reach threshold**
Because resting potential is more negative, about -100 $mV$ instead of -70 $mV$, the membrane has further to depolarise to reach the threshold potential. That means only a larger stimulus will trigger an action potential. Many normal stimuli will now be sub-threshold and fail.

Fewer, slower signals**
With a longer action potential and longer refractory period, impulses cannot follow each other as quickly, so frequency of transmission falls. The result for the whole animal is slower nervous coordination - slower reaction times, weaker sensation or weaker muscle contraction.

Final answer: Larger stimulus / larger depolarisation needed to reach threshold to generate an action potential. Fewer action potentials / lower frequency transmitted, so slower responses / weaker muscle contraction / slower coordination.
